The radar cross section (RCS) of the rough surfaces was measured in two fully polarimetric compact radar ranges operating at 100 GHz and 240 GHz.
Inverse synthetic aperture radar (ISAR) imagery was generated and analyzed to obtain the average backscattering coefficient (σ0) of each sample.
The RMS roughness of the unbrushed concrete, brushed concrete, soil, sand, and asphalt roofing shingles were 96 microns, 136 microns, 190 microns, 201 microns, and 137 microns, respectively.
The copolarization ratio (σ0_HH/σ0_VV) of the concrete samples approached 1 as the roughness parameter ks increased.
The backscattering coefficient of moist soil was lower compared to dry soil, likely due to increased volumetric scattering effects in the dry soil.
The backscattering coefficient of the asphalt roofing shingles showed an azimuthal dependence due to the organized pattern of the shingled surface.
On average, the backscattering coefficient was approximately 2 dB higher for the materials measured at 240 GHz compared to 100 GHz.
The moisture content of the soil samples changed during the measurement process, with the initial moisture content ranging from 0.03 g/cm³ to 0.23 g/cm³.
The particle size distribution of the soil sample showed that 96% of the sample mass contained particulates larger than 45 microns.
The average diameter of the gravel aggregates was approximately 10 mm.
The asphalt roofing shingle was attached to a 0.5-inch thick plywood sheet using standard roofing nails.
The backscattering coefficient of sand was within 2 dB of the dry soil sample for elevation angles of 10 degrees and higher.
The copolarization ratio of the gravel sample approached 1 as the elevation angle increased from 5 to 20 degrees.
The backscattering coefficient of the asphalt roofing shingles showed larger returns at lower elevation angles due to scattering from the shingle edges.
Future measurements will focus on better controlling the soil moisture content to understand the impact of both moisture and roughness on soil backscattering at these frequencies.
